title: Promises & async/await: chaining, errors and concurrency
objectives: Explain promise states and chaining: a promise settles once, and `then`/`catch` return new promises shaped by what their callbacks return or throw
Place a `catch` (or a `try` around `await`) where it really handles the failure, and spot a swallowed error, a missing `return`/`await`, or `return` without `await` inside `try`
Choose sequential or parallel `await`, and `Promise.all`, `allSettled`, `race` or `any`, from the dependencies and failure rules of the work
Predict when a rejection goes unhandled, and what browsers and Node 15+ do then

options.text: A **new** promise, settled by what `callback` returns or throws
`p` itself, so each `.then` adds to the same promise

questions.explanation: Every `then` (and `catch`, and `finally`) creates a new promise. If the callback returns a value, the new promise fulfils with it. If it returns a promise, the new one follows it. If it throws, the new one rejects. That's why chains work, and why `p` itself never changes: it settled once. `then` can't hand back the callback's value directly, because the callback hasn't run yet.

An async function **always** returns a promise, even when its body returns a plain `3` with no `await`. `+` turns the promise object into its string form, `"[object Promise]"`, and concatenates `1`. Nothing throws, which is why a missing `await` slips through. You need `(await getCount()) + 1`. TypeScript flags this one, because `Promise<number> + number` doesn't type-check.

questions.prompt: `const user = await fetchUser(id).catch((err) => console.error(err)); render(user.name);` — `fetchUser` rejects with "user service down". What reaches the error tracker?

options.text: A `TypeError` about reading `name` of `undefined`. The real error was logged and swallowed
"user service down", because `console.error` rethrows what it logs
Nothing: the `catch` handled it, so `render` is skipped
An unhandled rejection carrying "user service down"

questions.explanation: A `catch` callback that returns normally **recovers**: its return value (here `console.error`'s `undefined`) fulfils the next promise. So `user` is `undefined`, the code carries on, and `render` throws a `TypeError` that points at the wrong line. The real cause only exists as a console log. Catch only where you can act: show an error, return a real fallback, or rethrow.

questions.prompt: `async function getSettings() { try { return fetchSettings(); } catch { return DEFAULTS; } }` — when `fetchSettings` rejects, the defaults are never returned. Why?

options.text: The function returns the pending promise and leaves the `try`. The rejection comes later, outside it. `return await` keeps it inside
A `catch` without a binding (`catch {}`) doesn't catch promise rejections
An async function can't `return` from inside a `try` block

questions.explanation: `try` covers what happens while the function is running. `return fetchSettings()` hands back a still-pending promise, and the function (and the `try`) is finished. When that promise rejects, the caller sees the rejection. `return await fetchSettings()` waits **inside** the `try`, so the rejection is thrown there and caught. A bare `catch {}` catches everything: it just doesn't bind the error to a name.

questions.prompt: You need `user`, then `orders` and `alerts`. Both need `user.accountId`, but not each other. Which is the fastest correct shape?
questions.explanation: A step waits only for what it needs. The panels need `accountId`, so the user comes first. They don't need each other, so they run together, and the total is user plus the slower panel. One `Promise.all` over all three can't work, because you don't have `accountId` yet. Three awaits make the panels sequential. `forEach` ignores the promises its callback returns, so the code after it runs before either panel has loaded, and failures go unhandled.

questions.prompt: You fetch the same file from three mirrors. Use whichever **succeeds** first, and fail only if all three fail. Which combinator?
questions.explanation: `Promise.any` (ES2021) fulfils with the first **fulfilment** and ignores rejections unless every input rejects, in which case it rejects with an `AggregateError` listing them all. `race` settles with the first **settlement** of any kind, so one mirror failing fast fails the whole download. `all` needs every mirror to succeed. `allSettled` waits for the slowest mirror before you get anything.

questions.prompt: In a Node 22 request handler: `const a = slowQuery(); const b = fastFailingQuery(); const x = await a; try { await b; } catch { /* fallback */ }`. `b` rejects while the handler is still waiting on `a`. What happens?

options.text: The process exits: `b` rejected with no handler attached, and since Node 15 an unhandled rejection is raised as an uncaught exception
Nothing special: the `catch` handles it once execution reaches `await b`
Node prints a warning, then the `catch` handles it normally
The rejection is held until something awaits `b`, so nothing is reported

questions.explanation: A rejection counts as unhandled if no handler is attached by the end of the current turn. Here `await b` comes about a whole query later. Node 15+ defaults to `--unhandled-rejections=throw`, so with no `unhandledRejection` listener the process exits, taking every other in-flight request with it. Before v15 it only warned, which is the third option. Browsers would report it (`unhandledrejection`) and carry on. Fix: `await Promise.all([a, b])` (or `allSettled`), which attaches handlers to both at once.

prompts.prompt: Make the chain wait for the save, and carry a failed save to the next `catch`.
prompts.explanation: Inside braces, an arrow function returns nothing unless you say `return`. Without it the `then` callback returns `undefined` straight away, so the toast shows before the save finishes, and a failed save is a floating promise nobody handles. (Dropping the braces, `(draft) => saveDraft(draft)`, returns it implicitly.)

prompts.prompt: Make the fallback catch a rejected fetch.
prompts.explanation: `return await` settles the promise while the function is still inside the `try`, so a rejection throws there and the `catch` runs. A plain `return` hands the pending promise to the caller and leaves the `try` behind.

prompts.prompt: Fetch every user at once, and get the results in the same order as `ids`.
prompts.explanation: `ids.map(…)` starts every request immediately and gives back an array of promises. `Promise.all` waits for all of them and fulfils with their values in **input** order, whichever finished first. It rejects as soon as any one rejects.

prompts.prompt: Run every request, then pick out the ones that failed.
prompts.explanation: `allSettled` never rejects. It waits for every input and describes each as `{ status: "fulfilled", value }` or `{ status: "rejected", reason }`, in input order. That's the shape for "show what worked, report what didn't".

prompts.prompt: In Node, report unhandled rejections to monitoring. (Remember that adding the listener also replaces Node's default crash.)
prompts.explanation: Node emits `unhandledRejection` (capital R; the browser's window event is all lowercase, `unhandledrejection`). Without a listener, Node 15+ raises the rejection as an uncaught exception and exits. With one, it doesn't, so the listener must really report or deal with the error, or failures disappear silently.

snippets.question: What is logged, in order?
snippets.explanation: The executor runs synchronously, so `executor` logs first. The first `resolve(1)` settles the promise, and the later `reject` and `resolve(2)` are ignored: a promise settles once. `.then` callbacks always run as microtasks, after the synchronous `sync end`. The first returns `10`, which fulfils the promise the second `.then` is attached to.

code: const fetchUser = (id) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(() => resolve({ id }), 50));
snippets.question: What is logged?
snippets.explanation: `forEach` calls each async callback, gets a promise back, ignores it, and returns at once. All three requests start, but nothing waits for them, so `users` is still empty on the next line. The pushes happen about 50 ms later. Use `for…of` with `await` (one at a time) or `await Promise.all(ids.map(fetchUser))` (all at once) when the next line depends on the results.

snippets.question: What is logged, in order? (In an ES module, so top-level `await` works.)
snippets.answer: finished b, caught b failed, finished c, finished a
acceptable: finished b / caught b failed / finished c / finished a
snippets.explanation: `Promise.all` rejects as soon as `b` fails at 10 ms, so the `catch` runs right away. It doesn't stop the other two: they were already running and finish at 30 ms and 50 ms, and their results are discarded. MDN: "The other operations continue to run". If abandoned work should stop (requests, timers), cancel it yourself with an `AbortController` (next unit).

snippets.question: What happens?
snippets.answer: The process crashes with "Error: HTTP 500", and "still running" is never logged
snippets.explanation: The `.catch` returns a new promise, and rethrowing inside it rejects that promise. Nothing is attached after it, so the rejection is unhandled. Node 15+ raises it as an uncaught exception and exits before the timer fires. In a browser you'd get an "Uncaught (in promise)" console error and `still running` would log. Either way the error reaches no error boundary and no `try` up the stack. At the end of a chain, handle it (show it, store it, report it) instead of rethrowing.
